title: How to Build the Superhabit of Perseverance
author: Andrew Abela
summary: Andrew Abela presents perseverance as the superhabit for enduring difficult work, defining it with Aquinas as long persistence in any kind of difficult good. He notes that perseverance is the most viewed yet least practiced habit in his Grow Virtue app, which creates a catch-22 since growing in any habit needs perseverance already. He ties it to Angela Duckworth's grit, argues that perseverance alone predicts performance better than the full grit construct, and frames it as a mean between softness and stubborn pertinacity. Churchill's 'never give in' speech and Truett Cathy reopening a burned restaurant on Monday serve as illustrations. The practical method is self-distancing (the Batman Effect), ignoring tiredness so it loses power, and then taking very small, repeatable steps shaped by James Clear's four laws of behavior change. The trick, he concludes, is not minding that it hurts.
points: Perseverance is the habit people most want and least practice, so it has to be trained deliberately rather than assumed.
It is a mean between giving in too easily and persisting out of stubbornness, and honor and good sense keep it from becoming pertinacity.
Self-distancing, such as picturing yourself as an aspirational hero, makes it easier to persist through discomfort.
Ignoring tiredness weakens its pull, whereas resting at every twinge teaches you to attend to it.
Pick a hard but doable project, split it into steps of about fifteen minutes, and apply Clear's four laws to keep going.
quotes: Perseverance is the superhabit for enduring difficulties, especially ones that have a physical manifestation, such as tiredness or sickness. Thomas Aquinas defines it as “Long persistence in any kind of difficult good.
Perseverance appears to be one of the most desired and yet least tried of all the superhabits.
Perseverance, like many other virtues, is the mean between extremes. Perseverance is about endurance, and the extremes are not enduring enough and enduring beyond reason.
Once you quit one thing, then you can quit something else, and pretty soon you’ll get good at being a quitter.

If every time you feel tired, for example, you stop and rest, you will increase the power of the feeling of tiredness over you, because you’re teaching yourself to pay attention to it. If instead each time you feel tired you ignore that feeling, the feeling will get weaker.
The key to growing in any superhabit, indeed in any habit at all, is to take very small steps, repeatedly. Each step should be something that you know you can accomplish.
Break the project up into as many steps as necessary, so that each step is simple and brief, so that you could complete each in, say, 15 minutes.
